replacements.old: **Two regimes.** Starting from short synthetic oligos, the overlaps tile the whole target and the polymerase does most of the building; this reaches a few kilobases. Starting from existing double-stranded fragments, the overlaps exist only at the joints, which are exposed as single strands before annealing; this joins much larger pieces, is seamless (it leaves no scar sequence at the joint) and runs at a single temperature in one tube. The second is what makes assembly above a few kilobases practical.
replacements.new:
**Polymerase cycling assembly (PCA)** starts from short single-stranded oligos tiled across alternating strands. Their overlapping ends anneal and serve as primers for one another. Repeated denaturation, annealing and polymerase extension build longer products; a final PCR using primers at the two outer ends enriches the full-length construct. Overlaps should have similar melting temperatures so that all joints work in the same cycle.

**Gibson assembly** starts from double-stranded fragments with matching end overlaps. T5 exonuclease removes nucleotides from the 5′ ends, exposing complementary **3′ single-stranded overhangs**. These anneal; a polymerase extends the paired 3′ ends to fill gaps, and a DNA ligase seals the remaining nicks. The original enzyme combination uses Phusion polymerase and Taq ligase. A one-pot version runs isothermally near 50 °C; a staged alternative exposes overlaps first and then adds the repair enzymes, allowing control of processing for larger constructs. Joining is seamless because the shared overlap appears once in the completed DNA, rather than as an extra scar.

replacements.old: **Why the errors are random here but systematic in nanopore.** This is the key distinction, and it explains the whole design. In nanopore, the signal depends on a five-base window, so a given sequence context always produces the same ambiguity (Section 13). In SMRT, each pulse is a separate physical event: a nucleotide binds, is incorporated, and is released. Errors come from missing a short pulse or registering a spurious one, which are stochastic and essentially independent between passes. Independent errors can be averaged; correlated ones cannot. That is why SMRT can reach $Q30$ by reading the same molecule repeatedly, and nanopore cannot reach it by reading the same *locus* repeatedly.
replacements.new: **Why repeated observations improve accuracy.** SMRT pulse detection has stochastic errors that can often be reduced by combining passes over the same molecule. Nanopore measurements also contain random error as well as sequence-context-dependent bias, and repeated reads can improve their consensus too. The important statistical distinction is between independent error, which repeated observations reduce, and correlated error, which can persist. Neither platform has perfectly independent errors or a universal quality ceiling determined by its mechanism alone. Actual consensus accuracy must be measured for the chemistry, specimen and analysis used.

replacements.old: **Why confidence scores matter.** A prediction without an error estimate cannot be used in practice. AlphaFold reports per-residue confidence, which is empirically well calibrated: high-confidence regions are usually right and low-confidence regions usually are not. Low confidence is also informative — it often marks genuinely disordered regions (Section 23), so the model reports a real property rather than simply failing.
replacements.new: **Why confidence scores matter.** AlphaFold2 reports several complementary measures. **pLDDT** (predicted local distance difference test) assesses local structure around each residue on a 0–100 scale, with larger values indicating greater confidence. **PAE** (predicted aligned error) estimates positional uncertainty in ångströms for one region when alignment is fixed on another; smaller values mean more confident relative placement. Two domains can each have high pLDDT while their orientation relative to one another has high PAE. **pTM** (predicted template-modelling score) summarises confidence in the overall arrangement on a 0–1 scale, with larger values indicating greater confidence. Low confidence can be consistent with disorder or flexibility, but can also reflect insufficient information or model error. These are model confidence measures, not direct measurements or proof of a unique functional conformation.

replacements.old: **Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs)** combine antibody specificity with small-molecule potency. The antibody delivers a cytotoxic drug to cells carrying the target antigen, killing them by a mechanism far more potent than natural effector function. Three parameters are optimised: **where the drug attaches**, **how many copies** per antibody, and **how the linker releases** the drug — ideally only inside the target cell. ADCs are correspondingly expensive: a course of the anti-HER2 ADC Kadcyla costs of order £90 000.
replacements.new: **Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs)** combine antibody specificity with a cytotoxic payload. Design involves four linked choices: **which drug** to deliver, **where it attaches**, **how many copies** attach per antibody, and **how the linker releases** it. The payload must act effectively after delivery, while conjugation and release should preserve targeting and limit damage away from the intended cells. The suitable combination depends on the antigen, uptake, intracellular processing and drug mechanism.

replacements.new: **The trade-off across methods.** Animal methods provide affinity maturation but can be slow, restricted by tolerance to conserved self-antigens, and difficult when the target is toxic or poorly immunogenic. Mouse-derived sequences may need humanisation, whereas human-repertoire animals provide human sequences. *In vitro* selection allows targets and stringency to be controlled without animal tolerance, but useful candidates still need affinity, specificity and functional validation.

replacements.old: **2. Why coverage rescues it.** With 30× coverage and independent errors at $p = 10^{-3}$, a consensus call at a position is wrong only if most of the 30 reads are wrong in the same way. The probability of 16 or more errors among 30 reads is $1.4\times10^{-40}$. The consensus is therefore limited by *systematic* bias (GC bias, repeats, mapping error), not by random base-call error.
replacements.new: **2. Why coverage rescues it.** For 30 independent observations with substitution-error probability $p=10^{-3}$, a conservative consensus-failure bound counts every case with at least 15 errors, including a possible tie, as failure: $P_{\mathrm{fail}}\le\sum_{j=15}^{30}\binom{30}{j}p^j(1-p)^{30-j}\approx1.53\times10^{-37}$. Fewer than 15 errors leave more than half the observations correct, guaranteeing the correct strict-majority base under this model. Counting only 16 or more errors gives $1.44\times10^{-40}$, but omits ties. Actual consensus also needs alignment and insertion/deletion handling, and correlated errors or mapping bias can dominate these tiny independent-error bounds.

replacements.old: **What resolution means.** Resolution is the smallest spacing distinguishable, and it is set by how far out from the centre the spots extend. From Bragg's law, $\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$ with $\lambda = 1.54$ Å: 2 Å data requires reflections out to $\theta = 23°$, while 0.8 Å requires 74°. **High-resolution information sits at high angle**, where intensities are weakest — so resolution is limited by how well-ordered the crystal is, not by the instrument.
replacements.new: **What resolution means.** Higher-resolution diffraction corresponds to smaller spacings and reflections at larger scattering angle. From Bragg’s law, $\lambda=2d\sin\theta$ with $\lambda=1.54$ Å, 2 Å data requires reflections near $\theta=23°$, while 0.8 Å requires about 74°. High-angle reflections are often weak. Useful resolution therefore depends on crystal order, wavelength and angular coverage, signal quality and radiation damage; a better instrument helps record information only if the specimen supplies it.

replacements.old: **Why homopolymers are the characteristic failure.** A run such as CCCCC gives the *same* k-mer, and so the same current level, for several successive steps. The level does not change, so the only evidence of how many C's passed is how *long* the level persisted. Translocation is stochastic, so dwell time is a noisy measure of step count, and the base caller must infer "five C's" from a duration. This produces insertions and deletions in homopolymer runs, and it is a **systematic** error: it recurs at the same place in every read of that sequence.
replacements.new: **Why homopolymers are the characteristic failure.** A run such as CCCCC gives the *same* k-mer, and so the same current level, for several successive steps. The level does not change, so the only evidence of how many C's passed is how *long* the level persisted. Translocation is stochastic, so dwell time is a noisy measure of step count, and the base caller must infer "five C's" from a duration. This can produce insertions and deletions in homopolymer runs. Errors can be biased by sequence context and correlated between reads, without every read necessarily making the same mistake.

replacements.old: **Why that systematic character matters more than the raw error rate.** Raw single-read accuracy is around 95–99 %, against about 99.9 % for Illumina. Random errors average away with coverage, so a high random error rate is tolerable. Systematic errors do not: every read of a homopolymer makes the same mistake, so the consensus is confidently wrong. The worked example quantifies this.
replacements.new: **Why error correlations matter as well as the raw error rate.** For the illustrative raw accuracies used here, nanopore reads are around 95–99 % accurate, against about 99.9 % for Illumina. Independent random errors can be reduced by combining reads. Sequence-context-dependent errors can remain correlated, so the improvement need not follow an independent binomial model. The worked example contrasts that idealised model with its practical limitations.

replacements.old: **Why confidence scores matter.** AlphaFold2 reports several complementary measures. **pLDDT** (predicted local distance difference test) assesses local structure around each residue on a 0–100 scale, with larger values indicating greater confidence. **PAE** (predicted aligned error) estimates positional uncertainty in ångströms for one region when alignment is fixed on another; smaller values mean more confident relative placement. Two domains can each have high pLDDT while their orientation relative to one another has high PAE. **pTM** (predicted template-modelling score) summarises confidence in the overall arrangement on a 0–1 scale, with larger values indicating greater confidence. Low confidence can be consistent with disorder or flexibility, but can also reflect insufficient information or model error. These are model confidence measures, not direct measurements or proof of a unique functional conformation.

For multichain predictions, **ipTM** (interface predicted TM-score) assesses confidence in the relative placement of interacting chains on a 0–1 scale, with larger values indicating greater confidence; it complements the overall pTM score.
